sources: NPS Sonoran Desert Network wildlife monitoring report (2022)

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov's hiking guide, pets are not allowed on this trail; expect uneven footing and steps, and take it slow, since the trail sits at about 6,870 feet and the thin air catches many visitors off guard.
trails.didYouKnow: The paved section leads to a small exhibit building, and the summit overlook takes in the whole maze of rhyolite pinnacles that earned the area the nickname "Wonderland of Rocks."

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, pets are not allowed on Echo Canyon Trail; the Grotto is on the right about half a mile in, so turn around there before the trail starts its steep switchback descent into the canyon.
trails.didYouKnow: The pinnacles around the Grotto are rhyolite tuff, volcanic ash from an eruption of the Turkey Creek Caldera roughly 27 million years ago that welded into rock and then eroded along its cracks into columns.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov's hiking guide, this is one of the few trails where leashed pets are permitted; stream crossings can be hazardous during spring snowmelt or summer monsoon runoff, and the 1.2 miles is one way, so plan to double it if you return on foot.
trails.didYouKnow: Stafford Cabin along this trail was built around 1880 as a homestead, and Swedish immigrants Neil and Emma Erickson started neighboring Faraway Ranch in 1886. Their daughter Lillian ran it, partly as a guest ranch, until her death in 1977.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, pets are not allowed on this trail; it is the most exposed summit in the park, so head down at once if you see lightning or hear thunder during the July-September monsoon.
trails.didYouKnow: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the stone fire lookout on the 7,310-foot summit in the 1930s, and the trail passes through a short tunnel the CCC cut through pale volcanic tuff.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, pets are not allowed on this loop, and the park recommends hiking it counterclockwise (down Echo Canyon, back up Ed Riggs) for better views and an easier climb. Hailstone Trail is not recommended for anyone with a significant fear of heights.
trails.didYouKnow: Hailstone Trail is named for the hail-like spherulites embedded in the rock, small round crystal clusters that formed as the hot volcanic ash cooled.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, pets are not allowed on this trail; it climbs to a ridge, then drops into Picket Park, so you face a second climb on the way back. The trail ends at an overlook across the canyon, and there is no trail to the bridge itself.
trails.didYouKnow: NPS calls this the park's least-used trail, and the small bridge sits about 150 feet above the viewpoint across a streambed, so binoculars help in morning shade.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov's park guide, pets are not allowed and hikers should not start this hike after 1 pm. Hike the Heart of Rocks Loop clockwise by climbing the large boulders at the signed junction; NPS says the loop is too difficult to follow in reverse.
trails.didYouKnow: The 1-mile loop at the end of this hike threads through the park's densest cluster of named hoodoos, and NPS credits the Civilian Conservation Corps crews of the 1930s with naming many of the park's rock formations.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov's hiking guide, pets are not allowed on this trail. From Massai Point the route first drops about 400 feet on Ed Riggs Trail, then climbs 610 feet up Mushroom Rock Trail before the mostly level spur to the point, so save water and energy for the climb back out of the canyon on the return.
trails.didYouKnow: NPS calls the mostly level Inspiration Point spur a good place to slow your heart rate after the climb up Mushroom Rock Trail, and the spur is one of the eight trails strung together in the park's 9.5-mile Big Loop.

trails.trailTip: As of October 2026, per NPS.gov, pets are not allowed on any of the upper trails. Start early, carry plenty of water and salty snacks, and expect the steepest work on Sarah Deming Trail, which NPS says gains 880 feet.
trails.didYouKnow: The NPS route strings together eight named trails: Echo Canyon, Upper Rhyolite Canyon, Sarah Deming, Heart of Rocks Loop, Big Balanced Rock, Inspiration Point, Mushroom Rock, and Ed Riggs.

animals.whereToLook: Lower elevations around Silver Spur Meadow and Bonita Canyon Campground
animals.viewingTip: Watch bands from a respectful distance with binoculars and never feed them. NPS warns that any wild mammal can carry rabies, and coatis that learn to beg from people are a danger to themselves and to visitors.
animals.didYouKnow: Females and young travel together in noisy bands, while adult males usually live alone, which is why you often see either a crowd of coatis or just one.

animals.whereToLook: Lower Bonita Canyon, Silver Spur Meadow Trail, and along the scenic drive
animals.viewingTip: Drive the scenic drive slowly at dawn and dusk, when deer often cross. If you spot a fawn lying alone in summer, view it only from a distance and move on, because its mother is almost always nearby.
animals.didYouKnow: In a 2022 NPS camera survey of the park, white-tailed deer were by far the most-detected animal, with 448 detections, mostly at lower elevations.

animals.whereToLook: Lower-elevation woodlands and washes of Bonita Canyon
animals.viewingTip: Give herds plenty of room and watch them with binoculars. Javelina can turn defensive if surprised at close range, especially around dogs, so keep pets leashed where they are allowed and never feed them.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the pig-like look, javelina are not pigs; peccaries belong to a separate New World family.

animals.whereToLook: Riparian oaks and sycamores along Silver Spur Meadow Trail and Bonita Creek
animals.viewingTip: Listen for their raucous 'waka-waka' calls, then use binoculars to pick out the group; NPS notes that if you see one, others are usually nearby.
animals.didYouKnow: Family groups drill holes into a single granary tree and wedge an acorn into each one, building up a communal winter food store.

animals.whereToLook: Oak, pine, and streamside woodlands in the canyons
animals.viewingTip: Scan the oak and pine canopy quietly with binoculars, and never offer food. Hand-fed squirrels lose their wariness and can carry disease.
animals.didYouKnow: This Mexican fox squirrel reaches the U.S. only in southeastern Arizona's sky islands, but NPS says it is a fairly common sight in the park.

animals.viewingTip: If you see one, give it plenty of space and let it continue on its way. NPS asks visitors never to harm or handle rattlesnakes and to watch where they put their hands and feet among the rocks.
animals.didYouKnow: Adult males are often greenish while females tend to be gray. Both blend into lichen-covered rock so well that many hikers walk right past them.

animals.whereToLook: Oak, pine, and juniper woodlands throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: These social jays often seem unafraid of people, but NPS asks visitors not to feed them, so watch with binoculars, keep picnic food packed away, and stay well back from any nest during the spring breeding season.
animals.didYouKnow: A flock of roughly 5 to 25 jays shares a permanent territory, and many flock members, not just the parents, help feed the nestlings. Much of what is known about this comes from a banded flock studied every year from 1969 to 2006 at a research station in the Chiricahua Mountains.

animals.whereToLook: Sycamore- and oak-lined riparian canyons such as Bonita Creek
animals.viewingTip: Listen for its hoarse, repeated call and watch from well back with binoculars. Never use recorded calls to lure one in, and keep well away from nest cavities so the birds are not disturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: Trogons don't dig their own nests. In Arizona they mostly reuse old woodpecker holes in sycamores, and in 2025 eBird's taxonomy renamed the U.S. population the Coppery-tailed Trogon.

animals.whereToLook: Forested canyons and ridges throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: If you see a bear, stay at least 100 yards away, watch only with binoculars, and never leave food or trash unattended at campsites or picnic areas.
animals.didYouKnow: Bears are seldom seen by visitors, yet NPS wildlife cameras recorded 70 black bear detections in just six weeks of the 2022 survey.
